newsitem.title: UK: Europe Crude Outlook - Mildly bullish near-term.
newsitem.headline: Europe Crude Outlook - Mildly bullish near-term.

text.p: A yawning transatlantic arbitrage and gaping holes in North Sea loading schedules for early June should support European crude markets this week but thin margins and rising stocks will provide resistance, traders said.

With prompt NYMEX WTI futures commanding a premium of around $1.80 a barrel over prompt Brent, late May cargoes of the benchmark North Sea grade should have little difficulty attracting interest from U.S. Gulf refiners.
"The arb is certainly wide enough open to be hedging. There should be a market for Brent in the U.S. Gulf," said a trader.
Others cautioned that rising inventories in the U.S., where crude stocks jumped seven million barrels last week to stand 23 million barrels above year-ago levels, could dampen demand.

Dated Brent was valued at July Brent -25/-20 cents on Monday and traders expected it to hold that level this week, helped by a thin loading programme at Sullom Voe -- down some 3.5 full cargoes on May's already depleted total -- and on other systems.

Loadings from the eight main North Sea export streams are expected to fall by about 12.5 million barrels in June, equivalent to 260,000 barrels per day (bpd) less than in May, taking into account the shorter month.
Planned maintenance work is expected to take a particularly heavy toll on loadings of Britain's Forties and Norway's Oseberg crudes.
"There are only six (Forties) cargoes loading in the first 15 days and 22 in the second. Somebody has got to be short oil somewhere," said a trader.
And with no Oseberg cargoes due to load for five days in the second decade of June, most traders see little reason for spot differentials to ease during the coming week.
But last week's run cuts at Texaco Rotterdam's refinery and a further deterioration in margins could act as a brake on crude.
Brent cracking yields in northwest Europe tumbled to a two-month low of $1.16 a barrel on Friday.
"That may hold back levels but it won't pull them lower," said one.

A 50 percent surge in crude oil tanker rates for 80,000 tonne vessels in the North Sea, sparked by a dearth of tonnage for later this month, could also help prices for Norwegian and British crudes sold on a delivered basis.
"Freight rates appear to be soaring and this means the offshore loaders will probably firm as well," said a trader.
Conversely, fob cargoes could be pressured, traders said.
West African markets looked set to continue to benefit from steady demand from the Far East, despite a persistent deterioration in Singapore refining margins.
A South Korean refiner was said to have picked up a combined VLCC of Nigerian Bonny Light/Medium and Forcados late last week, continuing a spree which has helped clear out early June stems.
"It's only the 19th May and already there's very little left in the first half of June," said a trader.
